analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal right to full agreed-upon wages, mandatory paystubs, bigger fines, and longer deadlines to sue over wage theft.
analysis.headline: The Wage Theft Prevention and Wage Recovery Act was introduced on June 25, 2026 with 26 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill attacks wage theft — employers not paying workers everything they earned, through underpayment, unpaid overtime, off-the-clock work, misclassification, or withholding tips. It would require employers to give new hires written notice of their pay rate and classification, provide itemized paystubs, pay final wages within 14 days of a job ending, and honor whatever pay rate the employment contract promises. It raises fines for wage violations to as much as $250,150 per employee for repeat or willful violations, allows workers to recover triple the wages they lost plus interest, extends the time limit for suing from 2 years to 4 (5 if willful), bars employers from forcing workers into arbitration over these claims, and lets a worker's own testimony count as evidence when the employer's payroll records are missing. It also funds grants to community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers underpay them — especially low-wage workers in restaurants, construction, janitorial services, and home care, where the bill's own findings say compliance with wage laws can fall below 50 percent and wage theft costs workers an estimated $50 billion a year. The findings note women, immigrants, and Black workers are hit hardest, with Black workers roughly 3 times as likely as White workers to experience minimum wage violations. Honest employers who pay what they owe also gain, because cheaters lose their cost advantage. Law-abiding employers also gain a level playing field, since the bill cites law-compliant employers at a competitive disadvantage today.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give new hires a written notice within 15 days stating their pay rate, whether they are classified as covered or exempt, and the employer's identity, plus updated notices when anything changes [S2].

Every employer must provide itemized paystubs showing hours worked, pay rates, overtime, deductions, and who to contact — today there is no federal paystub requirement, which the findings say significantly impedes identifying wage theft [S2].
Final pay, including benefits, must arrive within 14 days of a job ending, and each day of delay after that costs the employer a full day's pay up to 30 days [S2].
Employers must pay the contractually promised wage rate, not just the federal minimum — the bill's findings say workers could previously recover only the minimum wage when shortchanged [S2].
Workers can recover unpaid wages plus interest and double or triple liquidated damages, and cannot be forced into pre-dispute arbitration or made to waive their right to sue over these claims [S2].

The statute of limitations doubles to 4 years (5 for willful violations), and the clock pauses while the Labor Department investigates, which the findings say previously cut off workers' claims entirely [S2].

Civil fines rise to as much as $25,150 per affected employee for an initial wage violation and $250,150 for repeat or willful ones, willful record falsification plus wage violations gets referred for federal prosecution, and criminal fines go from $10,000 to $100,000 per affected employee [S2].
When an employer's records are incomplete, a worker's credible testimony creates a presumption that their account of hours and wages is accurate [S2].

A grant program funds community organizations, unions, legal aid, and state agencies to educate workers, collect evidence, and partner with the Wage and Hour Division on enforcement, with priority for the most violative industries and areas [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in low-wage, high-violation industries bear the costs: new disclosure and paystub systems, penalty exposure up to $250,150 per affected employee per willful violation, triple damages plus interest, longer lawsuit windows, and lost access to mandatory arbitration for these claims. Taxpayers fund the grant program, which is authorized at such sums as may be necessary through fiscal year 2030.

drawbacks.text: Small employers face real compliance burdens: building paystub and disclosure systems in workers' primary languages, meeting 14-day final-pay deadlines, and paying up to $50–$100 per-employee fines for paperwork lapses under section 5 [S2].

The bill overrides the Federal Arbitration Act for wage claims and bars mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers, which employers argue will funnel more disputes into costly class and collective litigation [S2].
The grant program is authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' through fiscal 2030 with no fixed budget, an open-ended federal spending commitment [S2].
Doubling the lawsuit window to 4 years and letting worker testimony stand in when records are missing raises the volume and cost of litigation even for employers trying to comply [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: workers currently recover only about $3.2 billion a year against an estimated $50 billion in annual wage theft, and the bill's answer — bigger penalties, longer deadlines, disclosure mandates — is the standard enforcement approach. The compliance and litigation costs fall on employers, heaviest on small businesses in already thin-margin industries, and some of the penalty structure ($250,150 per employee per willful violation) is blunt. But because violations are concentrated among repeat offenders — the findings note one-third of employers caught stealing wages keep doing it — most of the cost would fall on employers who are not complying now, not on those who are.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the same day, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill in the House on June 25, 2026 [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, where it has remained with no markup, hearing, or floor action recorded [S4].
The bill's 26 cosponsors are all Democrats, with no Republican support recorded [S3].
The 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive, but a bill with no committee action and no majority-party support has never been scheduled for anything [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers are better off so far: the existing penalty structure, which the bill's findings call too weak to deter violations, remains unchanged, and the status quo persists with the bill stalling in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors are Democrats and the Republican-led committee has not acted on the bill; there has been no roll call, so no voting split exists.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, construction, janitorial, home care)
industries.note: These industries have the worst wage-law compliance — below 50 percent in some sectors — and would bear the steepest costs: fines up to $250,150 per affected employee per willful violation, triple damages plus interest, a 4-to-5-year lawsuit window, mandatory paystubs, and no forced arbitration. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the workers they currently underpay. The bill's findings note that one-third of employers caught stealing wages continue to do so under the current penalty structure.

Misclassifying employees as exempt or as independent contractors is a named form of wage theft in the bill's findings, and the new disclosure requirements force employers to state and justify their classification in writing, making misclassification easier to challenge. Temporary workers, about 25 percent of whom report wage theft, are specifically called out.

The findings state that wage theft puts law-abiding employers at a competitive disadvantage with violators, and the bill's grant program lists business associations as eligible partners, so employers who already follow the law gain when cheaters face real penalties.

industries.industry: Community organizations, unions, and legal aid groups
industries.note: A new grant program funds nonprofits, labor organizations, faith-based groups, and universities to educate workers about their rights, collect evidence, and partner with the Wage and Hour Division, with priority going to the most violative industries and regions.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee with no cosponsors from the majority party and no committee action rarely advance; the most likely path is that the bill sits without a markup and expires when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027. A discharge petition to force a floor vote over the committee's objection is theoretically possible but historically almost never succeeds.
